candidates.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
candidates.proposition: The context of 1 Corinthians 2 consistently concerns human authorities, so its rulers should be understood as human even if demonic forces also participated spiritually.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly hands the exchange to Jonathan, whose sustained first-person response continues through the contextual conclusion.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly contests the celestial reading of a principal Pauline passage and supplies the historicist interpretation of who crucified Jesus.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Carrier's claim that the passage favors celestial demonic rulers because human rulers would not knowingly thwart God's plan.

candidates.contextSummary: Carrier had argued that the rulers vocabulary is at least ambiguous and that comparison with Romans favors demonic agents; McLatchie answers from the passage's human context.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: Paul's title for James can denote a non-apostolic baptized Christian rather than a biological sibling, and its sparse, ambiguous usage does not establish Jesus's family.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator addresses Richard by name, and the ensuing extended answer presents Carrier's book-based grammatical and contextual interpretation.
candidates.loadBearingReason: James as the Lord's brother is among the most direct Pauline data offered for an earthly Jesus, so reinterpretation of the title bears directly on the motion.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: The historicist argument that Paul's incidental reference to James as the Lord's brother straightforwardly identifies Jesus's biological sibling.

candidates.contextSummary: The moderator presents James as an apparently unmotivated biological reference; Carrier responds that Paul calls all baptized Christians brothers and distinguishes apostolic from non-apostolic Christians.

candidates.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
candidates.proposition: The combined references to James, the brothers of the Lord, and Jesus's mother alongside his brothers support a biological rather than merely cultic relationship.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator directs the biological-sibling question to Jonathan, and the answer advances his interpretation across Pauline, Gospel, and Acts references.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument uses converging identifications of Jesus's relatives to defend a flesh-and-blood Jesus against the proposed cultic-title interpretation.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Carrier's contention that brother of the Lord merely distinguishes an ordinary baptized Christian from an apostolic Christian.

candidates.contextSummary: After Carrier explains James as a non-apostolic Christian, McLatchie argues that other Pauline and narrative references make the biological reading more coherent.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: First Corinthians 9 remains compatible with ordinary baptized Christians, while later Gospel and Acts family stories are legends and cannot determine what Paul believed.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator explicitly returns to Richard, whose answer addresses both the Pauline passage and McLatchie's appeal to later narrative sources.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This blocks the proposed cumulative family evidence by preserving ambiguity in Paul and denying that later narratives independently illuminate Pauline belief.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: McLatchie's appeal to 1 Corinthians 9, Matthew, and Acts as mutually supporting evidence that James and the other brothers were biological kin.

candidates.contextSummary: McLatchie has joined Pauline references to Gospel and Acts family traditions; Carrier separates the sources and treats the later names and relationships as legendary constructions.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: Acts is an agenda-driven work of fictionalized history that may use sources but reshapes them so extensively that historical facts cannot reliably be separated from embellishment.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Richard for his account of Acts, and Carrier gives a sustained description of its author, aims, literary method, and possible source use.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The historical value and authorship of Acts determine whether it can connect Paul to eyewitness traditions and an earthly Jesus, making its reliability structurally important.
candidates.contextSummary: The discussion shifts from Paul's terminology to Acts; Carrier characterizes its narrative as apologetic propaganda with reconciliation, political, and moral objectives despite possible source material.

candidates.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
candidates.proposition: Undesigned correspondences between Paul's letters and Acts support Acts's substantial historical accuracy and identify its author as Paul's traveling companion Luke.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator hands the question to Jonathan, who explicitly states his thesis and develops a detailed correspondence involving Timothy, Ephesus, Corinth, and Macedonia.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The argument supplies a positive evidential basis for treating Acts as companion testimony capable of linking Paul's world to the historical Jesus tradition.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Carrier's characterization of Acts as agenda-driven fictional history whose source-derived facts cannot be distinguished from literary invention.

candidates.contextSummary: After Carrier allows that Acts may preserve a skeleton of source material, McLatchie presents an allegedly unplanned fit between First Corinthians and Acts as reciprocal corroboration.

candidates.speaker: Richard Carrier
candidates.proposition: Source correspondences do not validate Acts because Acts contradicts Paul's own chronology and mission claims, deliberately alters material, and contains historical errors incompatible with companion authorship.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator requests Richard's assessment, and Carrier answers continuously with methodological objections followed by several specific categories of contradiction and error.
candidates.loadBearingReason: This directly rebuts the corroboration case and attacks the reliability and companion-authorship premise needed to use Acts against celestial mythicism.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: McLatchie's claim that undesigned correspondences between First Corinthians and Acts substantiate Acts's veracity and Luke's proximity to Paul.

candidates.contextSummary: McLatchie argues that matching incidental details corroborate Acts; Carrier replies that source use is compatible with alteration and contrasts Acts with Paul's statements about Judea, Arabia, and the Gentile mission.

candidates.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
candidates.proposition: Acts can telescope Paul's Arabian interval within its reference to many days, while undesigned coincidences and difficult external details cumulatively make wholesale literary dependence implausible.
candidates.attributionBasis: Following the moderator's invitation for a response, Jonathan addresses Carrier's Galatians objection and then develops cumulative internal and external corroboration arguments.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The move answers a claimed contradiction and broadens the positive reliability case for Acts, defending the bridge from Paul to historical-Jesus traditions.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Carrier's allegations that Acts erases Paul's Arabian mission, contradicts the letters, and merely mines sources while rewriting their history.

candidates.contextSummary: Carrier has listed contradictions and anachronisms; McLatchie argues that narrative compression resolves the Arabian chronology and that subtle convergences are too difficult for a late fabricator to reproduce.

candidates.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
candidates.proposition: Acts need not mention Paul's Arabian journey to remain compatible with Galatians, since its author may have omitted or not known that detail while preserving the Damascus-to-Jerusalem sequence.
candidates.attributionBasis: After Carrier presses the chronology in direct exchange, Jonathan gives the identified response defending compatibility despite Acts's silence about Arabia.
candidates.loadBearingReason: Resolving this concrete chronological objection materially supports the broader claim that Acts does not contradict Paul and may remain historically usable.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Carrier's argument that Acts places Paul in Damascus and Jerusalem in a way that leaves no credible room for his three-year Arabian mission.

candidates.contextSummary: The speakers examine Acts 9 closely; Carrier argues its sequence makes an Arabian sojourn unnatural, while McLatchie distinguishes omission from contradiction and allows incomplete authorial knowledge.

candidates.speaker: Jonathan McLatchie
candidates.proposition: If Acts was written by Paul's traveling companion, its thoroughly historical Jesus and the same author's Gospel are difficult to reconcile with the claim that Paul taught only a celestial Jesus.
candidates.attributionBasis: The moderator asks Jonathan to connect Acts back to the debate motion, and Jonathan states the companion-authorship inference in his ensuing answer.
candidates.loadBearingReason: The inference explicitly connects the Acts authorship dispute to the central question of whether Paul's Jesus was earthly or solely celestial.

responseIntent.earlierTargetDescription: Carrier's position that Acts is a later invented narrative rather than testimony from a companion who knew Paul's actual conception of Jesus.

candidates.contextSummary: After the detailed Acts reliability exchange, the moderator requests its relevance to Jesus's historicity; McLatchie argues that close companionship would make the author's historical portrait evidentially significant.
